profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal design review at a mid-sized ML research lab for the camera-ready experimental plan and system design of M-DESIGN, a retrieval-augmented model refinement framework for fine-grained neural network design focused on graph neural networks. The team already has a promising method draft and preliminary results on a 67,760-model knowledge base spanning 22 datasets, and this meeting is to review whether the current design is 'ready' for the final experimental push and paper lock. The agenda is to assess the evidence-graph construction pipeline, the adaptive retrieval module, the predictive task planner for out-of-distribution tasks, and the evaluation package under the stated strict budget. The expected outcome is agreement on whether to approve the design with minor changes, plus a concrete list of final experiments and implementation checks for the next week.

members.name: Dr. Lina Zhou
members.expertise: Neural architecture search, graph representation learning, empirical ML methodology
members.background: Lina leads the lab's automated model design projects and authored the original M-DESIGN concept note; she has a strong track record of turning exploratory systems into publishable empirical studies under tight compute limits.
members.private_state: She wants to approve the design quickly so the team can focus on polishing results and writing, but she is worried that last-minute redesign requests will destabilize the current codebase and jeopardize the paper deadline.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says the system is 'under the strict budget,' the relevant budget is the online adaptation-time compute for a new target task, with the historical knowledge base construction treated as sunk offline cost.
A 'case' in the claimed 26 out of 33 wins refers to each dataset-budget setting pair used in the current draft tables, because that is how she has been tracking headline results internally.

The 'OOD planner check' means demonstrating reasonable extrapolation on target tasks whose architectures are absent from the local retrieval neighborhood, not necessarily holding out entire datasets from the evidence graph build.
If the review concludes the design is 'ready,' that means the main system components and evaluation framing are locked, with only small implementation cleanups and reruns allowed.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: ML systems, experiment pipelines, reproducibility infrastructure, large-scale benchmark execution
members.background: Arjun owns the experiment orchestration stack and knowledge-base generation pipeline for the lab, and he is responsible for making sure the final results can be reproduced and defended during artifact review or rebuttal.
members.private_state: He wants the design review to surface anything that could create reproducibility or evaluation credibility issues later, but he does not want to appear obstructive when the project is close to submission.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'strict budget,' they mean the full amortized cost needed to use the method in practice, including maintaining or rebuilding the evidence repository and planner features for a benchmark suite.
A 'case' in the 26 out of 33 statement refers to distinct target datasets, because that is the level at which he organizes the runner and summary dashboards.
An 'OOD planner check' should involve dataset-level holdout or temporal holdout from the evidence graph so that the planner is not indirectly benefiting from same-dataset edit patterns.

If the design is 'ready,' it should already satisfy reproducibility review standards: frozen splits, rerunnable configs, and explicit documentation of how evidence graphs are materialized from prior runs.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts toward the strict budget
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to evaluating M-DESIGN 'under the strict budget.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats the budget as the per-target-task search/adaptation budget after the knowledge base and evidence graph infrastructure already exist.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 treats the budget as including the operational cost of preparing and maintaining the evidence graph and planner inputs needed to run the method for the benchmarked targets.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML papers, both online-only and amortized budget interpretations are common, and because both agree that the method must be budget-constrained, the phrase feels precise enough without anyone stopping to decompose offline versus online cost.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of the headline 26 out of 33 cases
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both cite the result that M-DESIGN gets the best performance in '26 out of 33 cases.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means 33 dataset-by-budget-condition cells in the main comparison table, where one dataset may contribute multiple cases.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means 33 target datasets or target-task instances at the benchmark runner level, each counted once.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'cases' sounds intentionally generic and summary-like, so both assume the other is using the same internal unit of counting, especially because the numeric claim already appears polished and publication-ready.

misalignment_points.topic: What the OOD planner validation holds out
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss adding an 'OOD planner check' before final approval.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes that the current leave-neighborhood or leave-family retrieval stress test already qualifies as the relevant OOD setting for the planner.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes that an OOD check naturally means holding out entire datasets or dataset-time slices from evidence graph construction to avoid leakage through historical edits.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both participants share the high-level goal of checking OOD behavior, and in research discussions 'OOD' often compresses several evaluation regimes that are all plausible enough to pass without explicit unpacking.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'ready for lock' permits after the review
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss whether the design is 'ready to lock' after this meeting.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes readiness means the conceptual design and evaluation framing are approved, allowing only minor bug fixes, reruns, and presentation cleanup afterward.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes readiness means the package is already reproducibility-complete, so only mechanical execution remains and no additional protocol clarifications or holdout restructuring should still be needed.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Teams often use 'ready' as a socially smoothing term during late-stage reviews; both intend to be cooperative and forward-moving, so neither spells out the threshold behind the approval language.

turns.inner_thought: I need this review to end with the design effectively approved. We're too close to the deadline to reopen core choices around the evidence graph or planner. For me, if it's ready to lock, that means the conceptual design and evaluation framing are settled and we only allow small code cleanups, confirmation reruns, and paper polish afterward.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. The main goal today is to decide whether M-DESIGN is ready to lock after this meeting, and if not, to identify only the last low-risk adjustments before we launch the final sweep.

turns.inner_thought: I should sound supportive, not like I'm blocking. But if we say ready to lock, I need that to mean the package is already defensible for reruns and later review: frozen configs, documented graph materialization, and an OOD planner check that would survive scrutiny. I especially want to make sure the evidence-graph pipeline and planner validation won't create credibility problems later.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. From my side, I want to review whether the evidence-graph pipeline, the planner validation, and the benchmark package are solid enough to defend once we rerun everything. If those are in good shape, I'm happy to move quickly.

turns.inner_thought: The strongest way to anchor the room is the headline result. Internally, 26 out of 33 cases means the dataset-by-budget cells in the current main table, and under the strict budget means the per-target adaptation budget, not the sunk offline repository build. Most of the real work left is just confirmation runs, assuming nobody asks to redefine the evaluation.
turns.utterance: At a high level, we're in a strong place. M-DESIGN is already getting the best performance in 26 out of 33 cases under the strict budget, so most of what remains is really confirmation runs and making sure the presentation is tight.

turns.inner_thought: Twenty-six out of thirty-three is good if that holds at the benchmark-instance level I track in the dashboards. I need to make sure the budget table and logs we archive line up with the runner outputs end to end, because that's what someone will inspect later. If they don't reconcile cleanly, we'll have a problem even if the top-line number looks good.
turns.utterance: The 26 out of 33 cases result is definitely encouraging. I just want to double-check that the budget table and the supporting logs are fully aligned with the runner outputs we'll archive, so the final package tells one consistent story.

turns.inner_thought: The budget story is clean in the way I care about it: on a new target, retrieval and planning reduce search substantially, and the repository side is already built from prior runs. I do not want this meeting to turn into a debate about charging historical knowledge-base construction against each target evaluation.
turns.utterance: I think the budget story is pretty clean. The adaptive retrieval is doing exactly what we wanted on each new target, and the repository side is already in place from prior tasks, so the final comparison remains well within the strict budget framing we've been using.

turns.inner_thought: I hear her saying the story is clean, but I need the practical end-to-end framing to be explicit in the package. When I say strict budget, I include what it takes to reproduce the method in practice from stored evidence graphs and planner features across the benchmark suite. And if we're near lock, those notes need to be part of the frozen package, not an afterthought.
turns.utterance: Right, and for the final package I'd like that same strict budget framing to cover what a user would need to reproduce the method end-to-end from the stored evidence graphs and planner features. As long as we write it up consistently, I think that will help us later.

turns.inner_thought: He's asking for reproducibility detail, which is fine as long as it doesn't force a redesign. To strengthen the paper, I can offer one more OOD planner check. In my mind, the current leave-neighborhood stress test already captures the relevant extrapolation story: the planner still behaves reasonably when similar architectures are missing nearby in retrieval.
turns.utterance: On robustness, I do think we should add one more OOD planner check before final approval. The current stress test already suggests the planner extrapolates reasonably when the local retrieval evidence gets weak, so I see this as a targeted final validation rather than a big new branch.

turns.inner_thought: Good, an OOD planner check is exactly what I wanted, as long as it's the kind that will stand up in review. I naturally mean a held-out setup at the dataset or temporal level, and I want it represented in the frozen configs so nobody can say we improvised it after the fact. If we lock, that config should already be part of the release set.
turns.utterance: I agree, an OOD planner check would help. Let's just make sure the held-out setup is represented in the config set we freeze for release, so it's part of the same rerunnable package as the rest of the final sweep.

turns.inner_thought: I should steer us back to the core system choice. The two-hop cap has been stable, efficient, and easy to explain, and I don't want anyone reopening graph-depth tuning now. If the headline table holds, that's enough justification for the final version.
turns.utterance: On the evidence-graph side, I still think capping the multi-hop edit-effect paths at two hops is the right final choice. It's been stable, it's easy to explain, and if the headline comparison table stays where it is, I don't see a reason to complicate that part any further.

turns.inner_thought: I'm fine with two hops; that's not where the risk is. My bigger concern is that the summary for the 33 cases needs to map directly onto the benchmark identifiers I archive. In my world those are distinct target datasets or benchmark instances, and I want that bookkeeping clean before anyone asks for exact provenance.
turns.utterance: I'm comfortable with the two-hop cap too. My main ask there is just that the final summary for the 33 cases maps cleanly onto the archived benchmark identifiers, so the top-line result and the exported records line up without any ambiguity.

turns.inner_thought: This sounds close enough to agreement. I want us to proceed as though approval is basically done, contingent only on the extra OOD planner check and routine reruns. Ready to lock, to me, means no further changes to system components or evaluation framing unless something unexpectedly breaks.
turns.utterance: Given all that, my view is that we should proceed as if the design is ready to lock once the OOD planner check and the confirmation reruns come back without surprises. At that point I think we're in final-sweep mode, not redesign mode.

turns.inner_thought: I can agree to that, provided the freeze list includes the reproducibility pieces I care about.
